utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good afternoon to you. Could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, you may sit down. Good afternoon to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, and also good afternoon to my learned friends of the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'm here together with my team, including Ms. Patricia Sellers, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and as our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink. Also later on during the session Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio will be present. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good afternoon to you. Appearances For Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us our legal assistants, Ms. Jasmina Cosic and Ms. Adisa Mehic, and our CaseMap manager, Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good afternoon to you and your team. Any preliminaries before we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an oral submission but I advise to postpone that whenever the issue will be dealt with regarding the Rule 70 witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wubben, and we'll come to that later. On your part, are there any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I should perhaps mention just in that regard that we did file a reply today. We worked all morning, so it was filed very much at the last minute, not with any intention in mind to surprise anyone but simply because it took us all morning to draft it. Yes. So that's been filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a courtesy copy by any chance?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, we were in such a rush that I have my own copy but we can make copies at the break. And we would also seek leave to rely to the Prosecution response to the Defence motion regarding Rule 68 dated 2nd December, 2005. That's one small matter which Your Honours can let us know later. And last week I indicated we would be objecting to the authenticity of certain Prosecution exhibits. Those are P600 to P609 for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Jones. Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It has to do with the submission by Mr. Jones. I take it that we will provide it with a courtesy copy as soon as possible and that's an urgent need for us has to do also with the oral submission I would like to do. I would like to be provided with such a copy whenever available, so that I can take a look at it, and we need an early ruling on this, and that's why I will take the opportunity even to leave the court for that purpose and later on address the issue as well. And in addition to that, we also filed recently - but I already updated the Defence counsel of that - of a corrigendum to our response by -- filed by Friday. The date of 2004 was incorrect and we should include the US government. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. All right. I thank you, Mr. Wubben. I'm sure that you'll both take into consideration what has been said and try to accommodate one another. Let's bring --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As I say, I'm happy to hand this over. It's my only copy so if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But I think Madam Usher, once she has brought in the witness, can help you. We can even get one of our secretaries to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. There are two ex parte annexes, so I'll remove those for these purposes and give you the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers, how much longer do you think you will require of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a series of video clips which I have timed in my office three times this morning so that we fit in between a half hour and I would say no more than 45 minutes. The clips are under a half hour, and it just depends on question and response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that more or less -- are we in agreement that we will just one -- two sessions basically with one break between, that we'll finish around about 6.30 or something like that, 6.15 or 6.30? Agreed? I want to make sure that everyone is in agreement. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I am in agreement with that, Your Honour, but you should be aware that Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio should come in and that might give us some minutes to change as he is not aware of the exact moment that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps Ms. Donnica can let him know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We will try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a break at 4.00; is that correct? Thank you. 4.00, which will be of half an hour. In other words, we will not be sitting from 4.00 to 4.30. And then we'll sit from 4.30 till quarter past 6.00. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I slightly overheard what you were saying. I would like to state something. It could be in the presence of the witness or without the presence. I think I can say it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, it can be. I would just like to state in open court, to Defence counsel too, is that Mr. Arria and I crossed in the hallway and he shook my hand and said, "Hello, Mrs. Sellers. It's nice to meet you." I want to put that on the record, okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that doesn't tempt you to -- or prompt you to renounce him as a witness, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's a close one but I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Ambassador, welcome back. Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we are going to proceed with your testimony, and I feel very confident that today we will conclude and you will be able to go back to wherever you would like to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And, Ms. Sellers, you may proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir, again. Yesterday where we left off we were speaking about your mission to Srebrenica, and I would like to ask that in terms of the insurgents or rebels, defenders as you've termed it, that you've met who were Bosniaks, Bosnian Muslims defending Srebrenica, did you only meet three of such persons or did you meet a larger number of persons?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I don't know whether you call them defenders or not because they seemed very defenseless to me. But there were three or four of them, and that's all the men, adults, that we saw while we were there. As I said to you yesterday, only women and children. So there were three or four. And the mayor of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, therefore I just want to make sure that my understanding is that you did not go to any Bosniak, Bosnian Muslim military headquarters while you were in Srebrenica on that day?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were informed there was none by the Canadian colonel in charge and the UNPROFOR forces that there was no military group assembly in Srebrenica while we were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you hear of either the Srebrenica army or of the TO of Srebrenica while you were in Srebrenica that day, those terms?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of them. We never -- as I think I said yesterday, we never understood there was an army as such, that there were resistance in Bosnia-Herzegovina and volunteers, but not an organised armed forces as such, that the only one that existed were on the Serb side plus the former Yugoslavia side. Those were really army officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You testified that you went to Potocari. It's one of the names that we could remember. Now, did you meet any fighting forces while you were in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only fighting forces that we saw in Potocari were Serbs and the UNPROFOR forces who were not fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. My next question is: Were you able to go to the municipal building, the city hall as one would say?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting took place in the -- in what I recall was the city hall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And that's the meeting where you met the villagers and you told them that you were there to protect them. Is that the meeting we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we were there offering protection, yes, by the Security Council, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were you able to go to the police station in Srebrenica during this visit?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Actually, we never saw any policemen. As I said to you, we never saw any adults, and my recollection is there was no police in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. And that would be either civilian police nor military police to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be difficult to recognise civilian police, as you know, unless they identify themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Ambassador Arria, right now I'd like to you watch a short video with us, and I'll preface this video by stating that it's P517. And, sir, yesterday you confirmed to us that after your mission in Srebrenica you did become aware that there had been a UN convoy that arrived in Srebrenica in the fall of 1992.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You confirmed to us yesterday that after your visit to Srebrenica you were informed, you became aware that there had been a UN convoy that arrived -- that was in Srebrenica in the fall of 1992, in the autumn of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers, my recollection is exactly the opposite of what you have suggested.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, then, Your Honour, let me retract the question and rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would just like -- don't take my word for granted, but usually I don't go wrong with my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ambassador Arria also said that he didn't remember that, so can I just clarify for my own sake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, when you asked him that question, he referred to his talks, discussions with Mendiluce and -- who never actually confirmed what you are suggesting and that rather explained to the witness that there was no such thing as convoys and help and assistance having been there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that's how I recollect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. That's precisely why I asked her to repeat the question because I thought I had responded precisely in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'll take that as your testimony and that's clear now. I would ask you to watch the video on your screen, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It's in Sanction, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, referring back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not at all certain that the subtitles we were able to read here had anything to do or corresponded to the words spoken, and we reserve our right to place an objection on this. I was unable to follow. It was quite difficult to hear. But I believe that what we were able to read in the English version did not correspond to what was actually said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers, are you going to refer the witness to particular parts of the script that we saw under the video or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm not. As a matter of fact, for purposes of this video, it is not the written word. What I will do is check that when we first entered this exhibit whether the transcript had already accompanied it and whether it was objected to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, my question after you have seen the videotape, is there anyone in that videotape you recognised as having seen in Srebrenica the day you were there?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was looking at the one with the blue jacket, but it's difficult, you know, to tell you a hundred per cent that that's the same person. It's already a few years back and I could have seen someone else. But the one with the blue jacket was the only one that seemed familiar of everybody that I saw there. And I don't know whether the one on the screen is Radic or not on the right side because in my screen it's not very clear. But that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I ask two things. To have the assistance of the usher to see if his screen can be made as clear as possible. I just want to briefly play that tape again and then I'm just ask the very same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, playing it again is what I was going to suggest. From the other point, on the other issue, I don't think we can do anything. I mean, we have had this problem last week, and I don't think there is a solution to it. We had a technician come in and not fiddle, but try to make adjustments and didn't succeed. Yes, just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can see it. If I stand up I can see it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is this, Ambassador, I mean, just try to follow this video which we are going to replay, and if you recognise anyone at any given point in time, just say stop and we'll stop there, we'll freeze the picture there, and then if Madam Sellers would like to put any questions to you, she will of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I caution you that when I said I recognise, actually, I mean, looks familiar but you know so many people that you see in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's start from the beginning, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Arria, do you recognise that person?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said he looks familiar to me in my recollection, but I cannot say that I recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And who would that person look familiar to or under what circumstance if that would be the person you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Sellers, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: He looks familiar to you. Can you remember whether you saw him in Srebrenica possibly on that date?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which date? On the 25th?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: 25th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was the mayor of the Srebrenica that you referred to in your earlier testimony?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a matter of jogging my memory. It's a matter I just cannot visualise him. But this is 1992 the picture that I'm looking at; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, sir.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I met him in 1993, and I wouldn't like to speculate on something of that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just note for the transcript I believe that Ambassador Arria is referring to -- the marking on the video shows 11.28.92 in terms of the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And the still we are looking at is at 04.00.4.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That will suffice with that video.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador Arria, you gave us quite a description of the actual living conditions in Srebrenica and the state of the people that you saw in the street yesterday, and I would like to ask you that you can confirm that you didn't consider that the manner in which the people were had any resemblance to normal life, any form of normality. I think that was the essence of your testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'll describe it to you again very simply.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If you would just confirm yes or no, because we're going to move to another video.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have precise recollection what you said to me yesterday, but I recollect perfectly well what I saw there. And what I saw was people in the streets, no shelter, no food, some of them trying to cook something on the streets and complete devastation. This is what I told you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I would like to show Ambassador Arria a series of three short video clips, and they are Prosecution Exhibit 427.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ambassador, I would ask that you look at your screen now and we will be seeing three short clips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers, we are hearing music but we are not seeing anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, once again, maybe I should state that these clips are offered for their visual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but there is nothing on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Oh. I'm sorry. Something has appeared on our screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We'll proceed to the second clip directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ambassador Arria, I would just note -- ask you do you note on the banner in this video clip that's being raised where it says "Ljilja Nada 1993 Srebrenica"?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We'll continue with the last clip, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ambassador, I would also like to ask you, did you notice that on the second clip there was a date that appeared at the bottom of the screen that said 9.9.93?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, in contrast to the people and the conditions that you saw in Srebrenica, or the people on the street, would your comment be this these three video clips we've seen represents more of a return to a normal village or community life?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could never say something like that. To begin with, you see the destruction of the buildings behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same destruction that you saw on the photograph that I took at the time. Many of those people were killed, a massacre, within two years of these -- less than two years after what you are showing to me. What I can see there is people hopeful that the United Nations are going to protect them after our visit and our commitment passing the safe resolution area which we were not ready to implement militarily to really defend them, and while -- the impression that I gave people in the way celebrating that maybe they have another chance for life, but never that they are back to a normal living. You can see, even though it shows great spirit, encouraging under the circumstances to be singing when all the buildings around you are burned and you hardly have any assistance from the outside world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I allowed the witness to answer the question having seen -- noticed Mr. Jones on his feet to lodge an objection, and I let him answer because I'm pretty sure that he could handle this question. But, of course, Ms. Sellers, you do realise that this is only what we've seen here, three separate events which can only reflect the reality of each of those three events and by no means the reality outside the building or the area where this was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's as if in a place which is -- where there is poverty and hunger everywhere but there is a handful of people who are different and are enjoying a nice banquet together with champagne and caviar. You show those and then you expect the witness to agree with you that life outside is as normal and as good as they are having it. I mean, come on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't -- no, Your Honour, I don't expect the witness to agree or disagree. I expected to elicit an answer from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But he wasn't there in September of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. But, Your Honour, also that's another question that I wanted to pose afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Let's hear Mr. Jones now, because I asked him to sit down when he wanted to make the objection because I thought it was better that way. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, firstly I take the point Your Honour said, but also Ms. Sellers' question assumes a great deal. In one clip, there was some indication of a date, but certainly this witness hasn't confirmed that the date on the screen reflects the date that is an incorrect year or anything of that matter, so one can't assume that this is an accurate -- this is 1993. That cannot be assumed. And her question assumes it. It cannot be assumed that it's Srebrenica, even if one clip shows the word "Srebrenica," I'm sure the word "Srebrenica" can be seen in lots of different places in the world. And so her question assumes that this is Srebrenica in 1993 for all three clips. And certainly the question shouldn't assume any of that, because that is not evident from -- it's not something within the witness's knowledge and it doesn't leap out from the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's another valid point. Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please proceed with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- this is cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- taking into consideration what I have just said, namely that I agree that the points raised by Mr. Jones are very valid.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. And, Your Honour, I'm contrasting a day's testimony with another section of a day. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. -- Ambassador Arria, you never did return to Srebrenica after your visit on the 24th of April? I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said he returned last year -- or this year, actually, for the anniversary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. During the time period of the war.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not possible to return.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. And were you ever able to? Even after you returned from your mission, you left Srebrenica from your mission, were you able then find out about information that possibly wasn't available to you during your mission, whether it be living conditions, whether it be police, Bosniak army, whether it be communications, were you therefore informed after your mission of various areas of Srebrenica life?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, very much so. We -- we -- since that moment the Security Council seemed to come to life again and to realise and to have to acknowledge publicly what was going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I mentioned to you yesterday, Your Honours, that for the first time the Resolution of the Security Council mentioned not both parties but mentioned the aggressor as the Serbian part. Yes, we were very thoroughly informed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So were you able to inform yourself at that period of time of any armed formations that were mainly of Bosniaks, Bosnian Muslims and Srebrenica, Srebrenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I told you yesterday on that respect that the information that we had at the time that the build-up, if you can call it the resistance of the Bosnian Maquis, had started. From our information, around 1994 was an increase in the build-up of resources that were not so far defenseless as they had been before. I was going to make a comment about the film, Your Honour, if you allow me. The photograph that I showed yesterday, I said that I took them myself and I delivered them to the Prosecution. Are these clips of the United Nations Protection Forces?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Beg your pardon, the clips that we just saw?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We're coming up to that video also that shows some United Nations Protection Forces. Right. I don't believe that the three clips that I've shown you here contain United Nations Protection Forces.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked that, Your Honour, because I said yesterday to you that the United Nations protection forces never shows a clip of anything that was taking place in Srebrenica. So I will be very much interested to find out if this was supplied by the UNPROFOR in any way, shape, or form to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers, if you wish to answer that. I mean, you're not being forced to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, I can back to Mr. Arria with that information. But I think the next series of clips will go right to the heart of the issue that he has raised. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Arria, can I ask you, did you recognise -- you've talked about the burnt buildings. Did you recognise any buildings in these clips?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said to you I saw some buildings in the back burned. Now whether they were in Mostar, in Srebrenica, Potocari, I cannot attest to that. Burned buildings, you know, look alike everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you recognise a school or part of a school that you had visited in this clip?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognised the one you showed me yesterday, not today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Now I would like to move to the last series of clips.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if would you permit me one second. Your Honour, this is clip P427.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ambassador Arria, do you recognise anything in that clip which relates to your mission to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what I can see are the armoured cars. The UN -- I think they are Russian helicopters and soccer field, but I don't know whether it's that same soccer field in Zvornik or is it in Srebrenica. It's not very precise. The one in Srebrenica I remember had some walls around where the people, the village were sitting up. I didn't see that there. But I recognised cars and helicopters. That's all that I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We'll go to the next clip, sir, and could you please watch your screen for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, did you put your hand up? Do you recognise --

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did recognise Mendiluce, I think, passing before. Not that one, before, Mendiluce, the Spaniard, the representative of Madame Ogata in Srebrenica. But that was before to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We can start the second one again. It's very short.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognised Colonel Radic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And, sir, which one is he?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's to the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have to go back a little bit. Do you recognise him there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which one is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one on the right side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Next --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the two UNPROFOR soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's me, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, I was going to ask you, do you recognise the man in the light shirt?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's me from the back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, is that you taking photographs?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to go back a few -- yes. A little bit more, please, Ms. Sellers. Yes. Let's start. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see myself there on the armoured car. I waving to some people. I don't think I was taking photos.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll look carefully.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So, sir, was it unknown to you that these films had been taken on the day of your visit to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, actually, I told Your Honours that when the UNPROFOR officers took away the cameras from my colleagues, they told us that they were filming, and I said to you that never, ever were those films shown at the United Nations when they should have been useful, which was before the massacre took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So, sir, you would agree that these films were taken and that it appears that you and another person in the tank were able to take photographs.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw myself because I was the only who had a camera. The rest of the members of the delegation, their cameras were taken away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I got the impression that in the second part it's the same person who has moved to the back of the tank.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct -- I stand to be corrected, but if you want we can see it again. I got the impression that it's the same witness, the same person who first was on the left-hand side of the tank taking photos from there and then immediately we see him in the back taking photos from the back of the tank. That's how I figured it out. Let him see it again. Perhaps he is in a better position to recognise himself than I am, because this is the first time I've met him in person. I've seen him on television before, but I wouldn't be able to recognise him from 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, it's a different tank. It's a different tank. So it's two persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: There are two persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So, sir -- Ambassador Arria, did you see the second person with a camera and the tank that appeared to follow you?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, could be UNPROFOR. They were filming. Now I can see they were filming. I wish I could have seen them and that the Security Council could have seen it, and I hope they were not as selective where it seems that everything is normal so that they could see the devastation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm ending the cross-examination now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he can recall where this is happening, when -- in other words, when he finds himself on one of the UN tanks or armoured cars, where would that be?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ambassador Arria, could you please answer His Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would it still be in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It is in Srebrenica. This is the building where we had the meeting with the people in Srebrenica. Now it was Potocari or Srebrenica, I have my doubts, because, you know, we're all the time going in these armoured cars. But the building was the building where we met. And, actually, when you see Ratko and all those other people coming out of the building, they were in the same meeting that I referred to Your Honours yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So when you had this -- in other words, according to you, this probably is Srebrenica town itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So do I take it, do I understand you that when you had this meeting in Srebrenica town on this particular occasion before you go on the armoured car or tank or whatever it is, you had this meeting in Srebrenica for which also the Serb military officers were present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I suggest -- as a matter of fact, I was going to try and refresh recollection by very briefly showing the first video clip with the helicopter and this one again, and I'm using it to refresh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I mean, we need to know this, Ms. Sellers, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw myself there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That's the question I was going to ask. Isn't that you coming off the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Hayes and then I saw myself. That's right, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is Hayes the person standing next to you?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ahead of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ahead of you?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's next to Ratko.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And you were wearing the light-coloured shirt again?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment I was the only member of the delegation present.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You testified you came --

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only one had been held up by Mr. Hayes, General Hayes in Zvornik. So I was the only member of our delegation there. For that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't know whether there was a question from the Trial Chamber, from Judge Eser for the second part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, what we want the witness to confirm is, having seen this again for I don't know how many times, whether this last part where we see some -- what appear to be military people and him and Mendiluce, he said he had recognised Mendiluce go before, whether this again is in Srebrenica on the 25th of April as shown on the screen or whether it's in some other place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ambassador, could I ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In Srebrenica town. Srebrenica town or village call it whatever you like.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: These two video clips we've seen now, did that take place, these shots in which you are in, in Srebrenica town on the 25th of April, 1993, the date of your mission?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you include in there Potocari as Srebrenica town?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. No, no. Potocari is Potocari. We're talking of Srebrenica town. Srebrenica town.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to say yes. I would say yes. But, you know, Your Honours, Potocari, I know you're familiar, I'm sure, is very close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it's ten kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So actually, you know, you come in and out. As you can see, we were in armoured cars most of the time, not all the time outside looking because this was at the end of the people of the village were desperate, asking for help. But we were in armoured cars. You know, if you asked me to swear to whether this is Potocari or Srebrenica, I wouldn't know what to tell you. It's one of the two places. I don't know how relevant that issue is, but it's one of the two places. And I also recognise the Ambassador of New Zealand and the Ambassador of Pakistan in the second -- in the last video, not at the heliport. Not at the soccer field.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But let's get this and the we have got some further questions Judge Eser and Judge Brydensholt. So basically the first part of this video when you recognise yourself on the soccer field in the proximity of the Russian helicopter, you would think that since you said that at that time the other members of the delegation had been held by Colonel -- Brigadier General Hayes that this would be Srebrenica, or would it still be Zvornik or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, within difference of hours I landed alone with Brigadier Hayes in the same -- in two soccer fields. But I have to believe that's the case you're telling me because Ratko did not land in the first time with us in Zvornik. So I have to assume that he was on the second stop which was in Srebrenica soccer field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Mr. Arria, you told us that according to your recollection the meetings you have attended took place in the municipal building. Now, on what grounds do you put -- base your assumptions that it had been the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At the time, we were not very much interested in the name of the buildings or what they were. We were led by the UNPROFOR people to a place where we could gather with some of the villagers, actually very few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the building in which you had met was close to other buildings or has there been some distance to the next buildings or could you describe what was on the other side of the street? Was it a big place or only a street, or how would you describe the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wish I could reply to you in the affirmative. What I can never forget are the people that I saw and the suffering that I saw. I wish I could also remember the names of the buildings, but unfortunately I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Eser. Judge Brydensholt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: You saw a building here and you saw some of those UN vehicles standing in front of it. Do you think, do you recollect that it was the same building in which you have had the meeting? You saw some people coming out, among them those uniforms officers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Do you recognise when you see those people coming out of this building, probably a Serb officer in front, do you recognise the Albanian -- the Serbs, the local Muslims, Bosniak Muslims, who took part in this meeting, are those local people among those we see leaving the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reason that I recognise the Serbs is because they were introduced formally to me by General Hayes with ranks and names. The other ones who were introduced to me like "my other friends". So it is, Your Honour, impossible for me to distinguish "my other friends" without being given to me the proper introduction of what they represented and if they had ranks, which I don't think at that time they had ranks, or what's the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: So even if you saw the clip again you could not tell us whether those people who are coming out of the building are those who participated in the meeting or not. You would not be able to, you think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only recognise Colonel Ratko, and I saw another gentleman who was with him, another officer, one of the Serb officers, and Brigadier Hayes. I didn't even see the Canadian officers in that picture on that video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Thank you, Judge Brydensholt. Ms. Sellers, back to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, as a matter of fact, my last question was just asked by Judge Brydensholt. I wanted to have him look at the film and if he could identify the three people that he is referred to in his testimony having represented the rebel defenders or the insurgent group. That would have been my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is no harm in going through it again, this last part, because there are more than three people who come out of that building.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, we're just going to look at that very last clip again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These first four persons in uniform and camouflage uniform, do you recognise how many of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you turn it back, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means. Let's take these two. Do you recognise any or either of -- or both of these two persons? Yes, but forget the one with the blue helmet on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recognise him. I did recognise some that left before but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay, all right. There are two who leave before who are in camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognise -- this is Ratko -- I'm sorry, can it be further down? That's Ratko. And the other one next to him is another Serb officer with Ratko, the one with the grey hair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And ahead of them, if you go ahead, was a British mayor who was actually my escort with Hayes at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see that. No, no. It's -- we have to rewind a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you start here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the mayor, and then comes Ratko, and then comes another of the Serb, and then it's all UNPROFOR. That's the ones I recognise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to have our case manager use her pointer so we can make certain who he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So, sir, which one is the mayor? Witness?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The one with the blue hat on?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one with the blue -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, 1.6.27.3 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The British mayor, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He's saying "major," I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was a major. That's Ratko, that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are at 1 hour, six minutes, 28.6 seconds. And he's the first one standing on the right. And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Next is one of his colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the same still, it's the second person that's being pointed with the long grey hair. The next one you don't recognise, you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Any further questions on this, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I have no further questions. I'd like to thank Ambassador Arria.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Ms. Sellers. Mr. Jones, is there re-examination? I take it that there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Firstly, Ambassador, I'm going to refer to something which you said earlier today which you were asked about, and if you will give me a moment, I have to find it in the transcript. Yes, you were asked whether you went to any Bosniak, Bosnian Muslim headquarters, and you answered: "We were informed that there was none, that the Canadian colonel in charge and the UNPROFOR forces by" - I think that was by - "the Canadian colonel in charge." Is that right? That was your information from the Canadian colonel in charge, that there were no Bosnian Muslim forces in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And also the information that the town had been demilitarised according to the UNPROFOR agreement at the airport of Sarajevo the day before that we got there, even though the Security Council didn't know about it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. If the witness could now be shown Exhibit D956, please. And while that's being passed up, Ambassador, you were asked yesterday about whether you received briefings about the situation, and you replied that you didn't receive briefings from the Bosnian army because you wished to be impartial, objective, et cetera. You did receive briefings, though, from the Canadian officer on the ground though; correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that we didn't receive briefings from the Bosnian army. I said that we never saw the Bosnian army as such, so I couldn't get any briefings. The briefings -- the only briefings that we got were from the UNPROFOR forces. And I could only add that Colonel Ratko in Zvornik gave me a speech about how they were in control of the whole situation, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And what you say Colonel Ratko, is that still Colonel Rodic or is it someone else?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Colonel Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if you look at page 13 of this document, the annex with your itinerary, firstly if we turn to -- in fact, I think it should be page 14. It says briefing by Lieutenant Colonel Thomas K.D. Geburt, commanding officer, 2nd Battalion, the Royal Canadian Regiment. Is that the Canadian colonel who gave you that briefing and that information?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm also -- sorry, if you keep the document and you turn back a page. When we see meeting with, we have Colonel Rodic and then three other names. Now, in the video we just saw, there was more than just Colonel Rodic in terms of the Serbs; correct? There were other Serbs besides him?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I could only recognise one, but the fact that we had the names of all of them is, like I told Your Honours, that they were identified to us as such and the others collectively they assign as friends, so that's the reason. Otherwise we would indicate them in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. So my point is this, that in the video we just saw, we saw other Serb officers in camouflage uniform besides Colonel Rodic and they were there but they are not mentioned in your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We only mentioned the ones whose names we had. We could not -- as I said to you before, we could not say and the other friends, you know, referring to the members of the resistance of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And just so we're completely clear, the people referred to as friends were on the Bosnian Muslim side. My point is that on the Serb side, and you described how the Serbs were in proper uniforms, there wasn't just Colonel Rodic. There were other Serbs in uniform who we saw on video but who were not mentioned in your report. I simply want a confirmation of that.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as far as these -- these three people mentioned there as being representatives of the Bosnian army, Zaim Civic and Madzic, firstly, are they among the people who were friends who were not in uniform?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat to me the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. You mentioned that Hayes said "these people are also my friends" and that they were defenders of Srebrenica. They were not in uniform. Does that refer to these people here who are -- where it's written Major Zaim Civic and Major Enver Madzic? Are they the friends?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that must be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And so is it right that although it says "major" there that they had no signs of rank on them?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said to you, unfortunately they looked very pathetic to me. They were presented to us as -- the friends were presented to us. They didn't look to us as a -- at all like an armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know whether they were from Srebrenica or from Tuzla or from anywhere? Do you know actually know where they were from?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember very well one of them said he was a teacher or a mechanic who was from Srebrenica. The rest, I don't know where they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. But aside from where they were actually from, do you know whether that day they met you from Srebrenica or whether they had come from Tuzla or from Zvornik or from somewhere else? Do you actually know whether they were based in Srebrenica or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they must have been trapped in because there was no way to get in, into the town when we were there. So they must have been inside the town, unless the Canadians, the UNPROFOR forces brought them in for this meeting because they were the only adults, as I said to you, from the locals that we saw during our visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So it's possible that they were brought in from outside by the Canadian UNPROFOR forces?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. And here they're referred to as major, as majors. Are you able to say why they're named as majors in this report? Did you verify that they were majors?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the -- you mean in the case of the Bosnia-Herzegovina people?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, the two representatives of the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I repeat to Your Honours, you know, they didn't look to us like a regular armed forces at all by no -- not even by the minimum standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Are we still with this exhibit or were you about to leave it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: About to leave it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just could you explain this meeting mentions people from -- representatives of the Bosnian Serb army and two men of the Bosnian army. Have you been aware that these Bosnian army people have been mentioned in this annex?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, yes, of course. As I said to Your Honours yesterday, I was the main drafter of the whole document. The annexes of the meetings of the people we had the cooperation of people from the United Nations secretariat who were taking names and hours and meetings, and actually was in charge of that was a lady called Miss Norma Chang, who was a director of the secretariat at the United Nations Security Council, and I saw her on one of the tanks now, the armoured cars. So on the names or definitions, they were done by the United Nations secretariat. I was responsible for the drafting of the document, not the annex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But regardless whether the ranks here are mentioned correctly or not, do you remember that besides these two Serbian people Radic and Popovic, said there had been two persons who have been considered as belonging to the other side, to the Bosnian side, so to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I said so yesterday that I -- my recollections are there were three or four locals. I think I identified one. I asked him, and he said to me he had been a teacher and also a mechanic. I also mentioned to you that they didn't look because they were not in uniform as representatives of any army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And that was a sort of formal meeting, not only just on the way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. This was when we landed in that soccer field, when I saw the triage, it's very interesting that -- for you, Your Honours, to know that that video shows us coming from the helicopter and doesn't show hundreds of people who were in the perimeter inside the soccer field being triaged by the Serb doctors. They didn't show that, which was really the most important part. I didn't see the importance of seeing myself coming out of the helicopter, but I wish the UNPROFOR would have shown the triage of hundreds of people around the soccer field being triaged by Serb doctors and not being treated by any doctors locally. That is remarkable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you finished --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- interrupting, only to state for the record in the exhibit that showed the film of your landing that we, the Office of the Prosecution, for purposes of today's presentation redacted and that certainly that segment is in there. So I don't want to have the witness misled at this point and we can certainly show it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for pointing that out. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we're going to need to break in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But just so this is entirely clear, you've said this many times but if you can confirm it now in light of His Honour's question a moment ago. These two people appeared not to be representatives of the Bosnian army but they did appear to be representatives of the Bosnian side. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And this would be a good moment for the break. I've got another ten minutes considering that in the end Ms. Sellers was about an hour and 40 minutes. It gave rise to a substantial re-examination I'm going to have to keep going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Take your time. Do you want to break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, isn't it 3.30?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The break is scheduled for 4.00, not now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies. I was misunderstanding. Okay. Well, that's much better.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, continuing from that you've told us, then, you did have briefing about the military situation from the Canadian colonel on the ground. It was suggested to you yesterday by the Prosecution that maybe you weren't very well-informed about Srebrenica or even the situation in Bosnia. Do you accept that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. Not at all. Actually, she didn't ask me, but I had bilateral meetings with a Spanish colonel, with a Venezuelan colonel who were in the area and with the British colonel who told me how scandalised they were by the behaviour of the UNPROFOR forces acting in such a subordinate manner to the Serbs and how ashamed they were of what was happening in the place, and I can -- my meeting with this Spanish colonel, what they call a mountain like the Canadian army mounted officers, this is the Spanish colonel telling me how horrible the situation was and how little we were doing, meaning the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you also receive information about the situation before you went to Srebrenica, both from the media and also from the UNHCR, Mrs. Ogata?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, Mrs. Ogata's memorandum, we only got it -- I only seen it 11 years later. The only information we had was the British journalists and the international media, the shots of Colonel Morillon telling the people of Srebrenica that he will stay there and would not leave them alone, which was not the case, as we saw later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, but just in terms -- I know you didn't see the letter from Mrs. Ogata, but just clarify for us, did you have conversations or any communications with Mrs. Ogata or UNHCR in this period, informing you of the situation?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only -- I knew her but I didn't have any contact with her until this happened. Only through her representative, which was Jose Maria Mendiluce, that I have mentioned several times, was, I believe, an extraordinary United Nations official.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that's from April 1993 that you began to receive information from the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From there on, we developed a very intimate relations, operational relation with them, and especially at the level of Mrs. Ogata, Mendiluce, and de Mello. As you know, Sergio Vieira de Mello, who later was killed in Iraq, an extraordinary UN official, was also there, and he became extremely important for us in getting information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And without mentioning names, is it right that at this time the UNHCR actually had persons on the ground, observing in detail the situation?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, Mendiluce told me that he had been reporting long before, not only abuses taking place in Srebrenica but on the Croat side by some of the Croat partisans, too. Actually, during our mission when Ms. Sellers asked me how we defined our own agenda, we went to Ahmici, if I pronounce it correctly, Ahmici where the Serb partisans had just burned, torched a whole family of Bosnians in Ahmici. So we went to see whatever tragedies were taking place that could have been shown to us at the time, not only on one side but on the both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I'm going to move to a new area. Just for the record, the historical record, I believe Ahmici was Bosnian Croats. Is that something you're aware of, rather than Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you a bit more about Brigadier Hayes, and it's simply because yesterday I rushed through exhibits in a rush to finish early, and as Your Honour said that I could go back now and introduce a few. Yesterday you said how you were aware that Madeleine Albright had actually even complained about Brigadier Hayes' remarks. Now I have two more exhibits quickly on this subject. One is an extract from a news article. It's 02110539, the ERN number. That's going to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I state then for the record that if this appears to be more of an expanded direct examination with new exhibits, that the Prosecutor certainly didn't function that into any cross-examination that was prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's cumulative, and I'm following on what Your Honour told me yesterday, that I could do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll deal with that, if the question arises, later on, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the title, it says excerpts from July -- sorry, this concerns excerpts from July, August, September, 1993, news reports, and I read, quote: "Newsday on 15 August quotes UNPROFOR's General Vere Hayes as praising the 'great goodwill' of the Serb commander General Ratko Mladic for leaving the peaks." And that refers to Igman, I believe, and Bjelasnica. "General Hayes added, 'There is still a military siege but there has never been a humanitarian strangulation of Sarajevo.'" Et cetera. And it's simply to ask you - you've already given evidence about this - is that, to your knowledge, the same Ratko Mladic who's been indicted for genocide by this Tribunal who Hayes is praising the "great goodwill" of?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can elaborate one second of this. It is not only disturbing to read that, but I would like to explain to Your Honours what are really United Nations forces and what they are not, why a man like General Brigadier General Hayes could say all those things and his commander, was a Swedish general, couldn't do anything about it. Because when the troops belong to the NATO powers, they are not United Nations forces. They are British forces, they are French forces, Russian, Chinese, or American. They become United Nations forces when they're made up of Pakistanis, Venezuelans, Primaverians [phoen] and whatever else. That's the reason that they report to the capitals and to the headquarters and not necessarily to the real command of the United Nations. So that's why the United Nations gets such bad ill repute for many things done by individual countries under the blue helmet but following the interests, instruction, directions and commands of their own. That's why a man like Hayes could act that way and actually commend a war criminal like General Mladic in front of the world and not be reprimanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just ask for an exhibit number for that exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D961, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You heard it, this page with ERN 02110539 will become Defence Exhibit D961.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now yesterday, also in the same vein, you referred to the assassination of Mr. Turaljic and the fact that the inadequate investigation showed in fact that Serbs could get away with murder. And I have an exhibit which I was going to use yesterday, and it's the same -- it's in the same vein and I'm sure it won't give rise to any problems on the part of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, but you may be wrong, Mr. Jones. I see Ms. Sellers --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Might I state for the record that the previous exhibit and the questioning in terms of General Hayes, and now the exhibit that I imagine goes toward the assassination, are issues that were not within my cross-examination whatsoever. It seems to be not a redirect of Ambassador Arria but a continuation of the direct of Ambassador Arria.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we will notice -- you don't need to answer. We granted this to the Defence yesterday at a certain point in time when we decided to continue today with his testimony, because we had asked Mr. Jones to cut short and finish in two hours, on the assumption that you would be able to finish within the rest of the time allocated. At that point in time when you needed more time than you had indicated or we had indicated in the first place, we decided -- we agreed that we would allow Mr. Jones put the questions that he had renounced to because of the time restriction that we had imposed. So this is the situation. Of course, now that he is putting the question and he is bringing in new documents, if you want to deal with these later on, of course -- I mean, we are not -- we are not going to say no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to reserve my right for now re-cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I don't think Mr. Jones will oppose that in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have notified this list already. I mean, the Prosecution is aware of these exhibits and it is entirely in the spirit that Your Honour mentioned that I'm dealing with this now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Simply this: You told us how you commissioned a report into the adequacy of the investigation. Is this the document which is being put in front you, is that the report or the reports?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just ask for an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document, which consist of a number of pages, starting with ERN 0090972 and inclusive of 009113 is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D962.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now just a few last matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You were shown these videos, obviously, today of people. I won't say anything more about that. Of people doing various things. Now, it was suggested -- it's been suggested to you that in fact this showed that everyone was happy and that everything was fine in Srebrenica after your departure. In light of what you know about the situation in Srebrenica, is that a realistic suggestion, that in April 1993 things were as you described? In 1995 there was a genocide, but in between everyone was happy and everything was fine; does that seem realistic to you?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, Your Honours, thinking when I saw these videos this was six months after we were there. By that time Srebrenica was very much in the limelight of public -- international public opinion. Our visit had, of course, an impact on the behaviour of the -- of the Serb forces that were attacking the area, and things got improved. No doubt people, when they think they're going to live longer, they celebrate. That was the impression that I got, and that was my first spontaneous comment to you, that they looked to me like people celebrating they're going to live another day. But of course they didn't look to me like they were celebrating life when the whole town was destroyed. And actually, Your Honour, even if you go today - I was there for the tenth anniversary of the massacre - it's still very much destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you spoke at length yesterday about revisionism, moral equivalence, about the interest of the international community in burying the truth about Srebrenica. Do you see that suggestion that everything was fine in Srebrenica as part of that revisionism?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will respond, you know, with a very personal feeling about it. I wrote an article, Your Honours, for The Los Angeles Times at the time which I call "Haiti, The Black Bosnia," in which I said that Europeans treated the Bosnians as Muslims and not as Europeans and the Latin Americans treated Haiti as blacks and not as Latin Americans. Both reprehensible attitudes by both regions. And the -- in the case of Bosnia, suddenly it became very easy to eliminate the problem, treating them with this, I would say, a moral equality of the parties in which aggressors and victims were treated the same and accorded the same treatment. Even better treatment but give -- provided to the aggressors than to the victims by the respect that was shown by United Nations UNPROFOR forces, and actually even in some representatives on the ground, which was the case of Mr. Akashi, which was so deferential in his treatment, and actually even in the Dutch report is very strong on the behaviour of some of its officers, and I was a witness to that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And finally you were shown this film, which apparently was shot by UNPROFOR, of your mission, the debut in Srebrenica. Does that -- do those photographs, do they depict the plight of Srebrenica? Do they accurately show the suffering which you've described there?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The video or the photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies; the video.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The video is a cover-up. The video - and I'm sorry to say - is another cover-up to try to portray it into the form [indiscernible]. I'm really ashamed to believe that it was done by the United Nations I was so proud to be a part of. And I find it reprehensible that they could take a film of people suffering, and if they're celebrating one more day of their lives and to only selectively choose that event of people celebrating their life and hiding the suffering and the misery of that town, I find that really detestable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is, of -- I think we are --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, two points. No, I understand exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And I think you head in the right direction because I think we have a mixup with one video and another here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I take the point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is no indication that the videos from which we saw three clips of celebrations, marches with women in front, banners et cetera, was shot by the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, I never got that indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In case there's any confusion, I'm referring to the video showing you and the others in Srebrenica on APCs, and I'm wondering whether that video, whether that shows the suffering and the plight of the Srebrenicans that you saw or not.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. It looked a tourist visit to a town escorted by the United Nations force.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Do you want to re-cross again the witness on any of the issues touched by Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the videos, the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The new exhibits basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the temptation is very great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the restraint is remarkable.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And what would I like to say is that the Prosecutor will preserve its rights to look at the evidence under other circumstances, and for expediency, and I understand this has been quite prolonged, that we will at this point waive our right for re-cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. It's not a question of waive or not waive. It's a question please decide whether you want to put some further questions or not. I mean, it's not question of renouncing. I mean, because I don't think I can leave that open and in two weeks' time or one month's time you will say now we want Mr. Ambassador back to put some more questions to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
