On Friday -- at the very last minute on Friday -- Your Honours had ordered that they file a response by Friday, but at 4.30 p.m. it was filed, so we didn't have it for weekend. If they had been diligent for once, then in fact we would have had that -- the whole weekend. We could have filed a reply yesterday rather than instead after court last night and this morning me having to -- to draft a reply. And I really find it intolerable that the Prosecution seeks to blame us for a remarkable lack of diligence on their part, months and months going by without them pursuing this. And a party cannot rely on its own defaults in litigation, and it's the Prosecution which has brought us to this juncture where we're scrambling about at the last minute to come up with a solution. And I would really ask Your Honours to be firm with the Prosecution and to put your foot down. I'm familiar with criminal -- in criminal trials Judges bending over backwards to help the Defence, but I'd ask you not to bend over backwards to help the Prosecution. They've created this mess, and they've got to live with it. As far as the actual merits of what Mr. Wubben has said are concerned, firstly, as I said, it's completely unmeritorious the argument that the USG is saying that we shouldn't be present at the interview. As I say, we're waiting for a reply as to whether the witness himself would request our presence so as to maintain good relations which we have with him already. Now, I move to the main body of my reply to Mr. Wubben's submissions. Firstly, their position, actually, is that the Trial Chamber has no jurisdiction in this matter really, that it is none of your business, according to the Prosecution, whether they contact a witness. That's their current position, and I'm surprised that Mr. Wubben perhaps tactfully decided not to argue that this is none your of your business. We say it's very much your business in part of ensuring a fair trial. It's a fundamental obligation of your Trial Chamber, and so of course you have a right to rule on this. As far as -- and as far as the -- as what happened last Tuesday is concerned, to a certain extent that's -- that's water under the bridge, but in front of the three of us Mr. Wubben said when we asked, "Do you have authorisation?" he said, "We have it," and he said something about, "Read the decision." He did not say, "We don't need it." He absolutely did not say, "We don't need authorisation," and that was the representation which led to contacts which we made. Now, paragraph by paragraph. First, Mr. Wubben referred to paragraph 4 of our response, and he said that all of the cases cited concern subpoenas or something of that matter. Well, that's not -- that's simply not true. I'm not going to go through the decisions at length now, but we've made very careful submissions on these cases, and Your Honours will have to look at those cases and you'll see that it's not -- that they're all on subpoena. And even if they are, of course -- I mean, even if some of them concern subpoena, of course analogous reasoning applies in different matters, and it's not as if subpoena decisions are completely separate from any other type of decision. Of course it's relevant what's stated there and what we've cited. Responding to paragraph 6, Mr. Wubben said, "Well, we say that Article 18 of the Statute only goes to investigations." Well, there's Article 16 of the Statute, which -- which means the Prosecution has duties throughout the trial. Well, that completely misses the point, the main thrust of our point, which is that the particular power of the Prosecution to interview witnesses is to do with investigations. And when we're at trial -- and we're not just at trial here. I mean, the Prosecution's case is closed. It closed months ago. So they're not investigating when they seek to interview Dudley. They're purely and simply trying to -- well, I'll wait until Your Honour has dealt with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have a very short break. I take it that you don't have much more to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: About ten minutes, five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, five minutes, because they have only got a minute and half on the tape, so and they need to change the tape, and we'll finish in about five minutes' time afterwards. Yes, we are stopping here until they change the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Okay. MADAM USHER: All rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, we're staying right here. We're anxious to rise, I can assure you. Okay. I see the thumbs-up signal. Mr. Wubben, in the meantime we were discussing. If we were to suggest to you as food for thought and then tell us when we finish that without prejudice to any pretended right that you claim, and on the understanding that if you would accept that we are going to suggest this would not constitute a precedent for the future, would you accept that in this particular case if this Major Dudley interviewed that will be done in the presence of the Defence? Reserve your answer and tell us later on. And it will be recorded that this is being done without prejudice and definitely in a way which would not establish a precedent. Mr. Jones, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Try to -- I mean, I am not imposing on you, but we promised everyone to finish at 6.15 to 6.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll go as quickly as I can. Yes. The point about Article 18 of the Statute is that -- is that the purpose clearly is not to investigate this witness to see if he's a potential witness. It's to gain a tactical advantage in the trial process, namely to be able to surprise us during cross-examination by popping up and mentioning a matter which the Prosecution had explored with the witness and which we're unaware of, and that is simply unfair to the Defence from any view that that should be allowed to happen. And, Your Honour, Mr. Wubben's submission appears to be that even though this is one week before the witness is due to travel, although he's making travel plans --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can forget that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- that -- that's irrelevant, but the case law doesn't say it's irrelevant. There's a factual matrix --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Everything's relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Everything's relevant. Thank you, Your Honour. He referred to paragraph 9 in his submissions regarding the witness's position. We're trying to ascertain the witness's position. But I would ask you to consider that it is difficult for us to have the sort of contacts we would normally have with a witness because we always go through a government, and that's impeded, as I say, our normal practice to actually find out what our witness's position would be. And also given the witness's status as a former member of the military, if he's contacted by his government with a request, he may well feel that he has no say in the matter. It may not be easy for him to say, "Well, I want the Defence to be there," or, "I'm not happy about this." And in that light, you have to consider how important it is the rapport we have in our relations with a witness, and that's why, to the point which I'm coming to in a moment, but if you can picture a witness who arrives here, when we're proofing him, of course one thing, as I mention in our motion, we want to prepare for possible cross-examination. We're going to be proofing him with representatives of the US government there. Now, if we seek to anticipate with the witness what might come up, what he might know about which -- something which would be of interest to us, but we have this -- this terrible barrier that he knows some things based on questions or documents put by the Prosecution which we don't know about, and he's worried that he shouldn't divulge that, and the US government representative is going to interject and say, "Well, we can't -- he can't really answer that because that might divulge what the Prosecution asked him two days ago," you can see the potential for utterly messing up our plans. Whereas if we're there for the interview and if we don't ask any questions, we stay silent and behave ourselves, what possible damage is there? And then we have a perfectly open relationship with our -- the witness we're calling. We know what he was asked about. We know what to explore, and it's abundantly clear that the reason why the Prosecution don't want us there is because they don't want us to know what might come up. Time and again Mr. Wubben says -- reiterates there should be no surprise, no ambush, but they're always trying to catch us by surprise. Mr. Wubben is the high priest of surprise. He's always trying to mention something at the last minute or spring something on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I protest, Your Honour. This is really inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: There is even I think a very recent practice direction of this very Tribunal regarding the conduct of the -- of Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I am really grieved by this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. Wubben. Let's keep to the arguments proper. Do you -- there is a specific request for rescheduling adjournment or delaying the scheduled testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's huge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you object to that as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Enormously object to it, Your Honour. Because it's not only the inconvenience of our scheduling of when witnesses are to arrive, et cetera, but we actually -- we've planned our witnesses, the sequence of witnesses, the exhibits we're going to use, the sequences very carefully, and just to have a witness all of a sudden disappear off the screen for a while and come back months later is extremely disruptive to our presentation. And there is actually even a sequence of -- as I say, of exhibits which are planned with the witness. And that's why also we fear that this -- the timing of this request destabilises our preparation. It's already destabilising us in that a day and a half which I would have used to be preparing for the witness has been lost. I did have a couple of final matters. And by -- Your Honour, I take it that you don't take my remark -- it was a flippant remark and I apologise if it was mistaken, but I trust Your Honour doesn't regard what I said a moment ago as being a grave matter. Paragraph 10 of our response, Mr. Wubben said that the Halilovic appeals decision concerns subpoena. My submission is that you can apply the reasoning by analogy that if it's only to be able to prepare better for cross-examination that is not a sufficient reason to grant a request for contact. That was my point. On paragraph 11, Mr. Wubben said, again, that the fact that the final travel plans have been laid --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You already mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, this is a slightly different point, Your Honour. That since the United States government and the witness didn't object that that shows that there is no problem. But those -- the United States government doesn't have a duty to ensure a fair trial. They don't have a duty to ensure that the rights of the accused are respected. So, of course, one can't point to the US government and say, well, they've decided that that's all right. That's a matter for Your Honours to decide whether the timing would actually interfere with our preparation. And that also goes to the point about leaking a Rule 70 material. The United States government isn't there to police, even though they say that they will try to, but they don't know the whole context of this trial. They don't know what might be termed confidential, whereas we do know, and if we're there, then of course we can react. Another reason why we should be present. Paragraph 19 refers to a separate problem, namely disclosure of the list of topics which the Prosecution wish to raise, and that is it is a genuine problem, and I'm sure that Your Honour will appreciate it. That we technically could be stopped from re-examining on issues on which the Prosecution has cross-examined unless we get the USG's permission beforehand to re-examine on those matters, and so we'll need to know what the list is beforehand so we can seek that permission. As far as ex parte matters are concerned, I've divulged the content pretty much of our two annexes, and I trust the Prosecution will do the same. Basically I would implore Your Honours to put your foot down and to -- to penalise, if need be, the Prosecution for this delay and certainly to do your utmost to ensure that the rights of the accused are respected by our presence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Three things. When is in witness arriving in The Hague? Or when is he scheduled to arrive?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The 8th, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The 8th is when? Today is the 6th, so it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thursday. Thursday. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Travelling on the 7th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's number 1. Number two: If you have a response at any time between now and tomorrow when we are sitting from the US embassy with regard to the request you put to them to get hold of Major Dudley and put to him the practice that you adopt, please communicate it to us -- to the Prosecution and to us as early as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As early as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's number two. Number three: Just in case if you are in a position to give us a very quick yes or no feedback to the request that we made, whether you would be prepared -- no explanations required. It's either a yes or a no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Then it is a no, because I would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's all. We don't need an explanation. It's just your answer is no. All right. We will hope to be -- yes, Judge Eser. Try to be as short as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Yes, I will try to be as short of possible. But in order to get to the gist of the problem, now I have a question of the Defence. If the Prosecution would have wanted to interview this witness, let's say a month ago, would it have been a problem that the Defence -- the Prosecution to meet prior to your interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, it would still be a problem if we were to be absent, if that's what Your Honour is asking. The problem is exacerbated by the shortness of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But there are two questions: Whether it's necessary, according to your opinion, that the witness is interviewed after the Defence; or whether it might be allowable that he's interviewed before the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, it's slightly difficult to answer, Your Honour, because without giving too much away, obviously we've had prior interviews in the past with the witness, so we've already obviously interviewed him however long, a year ago or whenever it was. If Your Honour is asking if the Prosecution had interviewed Colonel Dudley before we had even heard of him or knew of his existence or contacted him, then of course that would pose no problem. The problem is posed in the circumstances such as they are. In fact, I've remembered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just to take the case that you have put the witness on your witness list, the Defence witness list, and then the Prosecution would decide to interview this witness without telling the Defence that they are going to do so, would that be acceptable according to your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. No, I think once he's on the witness list, that's a decisive -- that's a decisive moment and no case law says that that -- that is -- is a relevant factor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I -- sorry, it's just that I have remembered one other point I wanted to make. The Prosecution did say that there's still a possibility that Colonel Dudley could be a witness for them perhaps in rejoinder. To me that's a ridiculous suggestion, because if he's here and we cross-examine him the idea that he could then be called to rebut something which he's already said and has been cross-examined upon, I've never heard of that ever happening. So I also wanted to say that that doesn't make any sense to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So what, is your position as soon as a witness is put on -- either on the Prosecution list or the witness of course would go for both sides, if he was put on the Defence witness list, that then it will only allowable to interview him in the presence of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not making any -- I don't want to make any dogmatic categorical idea that there is -- yes, yes. But I simply would say -- I'm not saying there's any particular moment at which something distinctively where the rules change, that they're hard and fast rules, there's a factual matrix into which all these things must be put, and that's it's simply that. I'm not arguing for an ironclad rule one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. I thank you both. And I wish to express my gratitude to you, Madam Reporter, for having been patient with us. Unfortunately, we couldn't finish earlier. The interpreters, of course, and the rest of the staff, I thank you so much. Tomorrow we hope to be able to come down with our decision which of course will need to be oral for the time being and then if we feel it is necessary, we will try and follow it up with a written one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 7th day of December, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.
